summary: A preliminary discussion of Pcmail, a distributed mail system for personal computers. A central repository stores incoming mail and keeps a stable copy of each user's mail state, while the users' PCs act as clients. It was published for discussion, is not a standard, and was replaced by RFC 993.

eli5.summary: Your computer is sometimes off, so a big shared mailbox at a central place holds your letters until your computer turns on and asks for them.

questions: how does a mail repository work for personal computers
subtitle: A distributed mail system architecture for personal computers with a central repository

tldr.problem: Personal computers are inexpensive and portable, but have limited storage and intermittent network access. Users wanted to access mail from multiple PCs without storing everything locally or requiring constant connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: PCMAIL divides mail storage into a central repository server and multiple PC clients. The repository stores all mail and maintains the authoritative mail state. Each client maintains a local copy and synchronizes via the Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP). Messages are split into tiny summaries (descriptors) and bodies so clients can view summaries even with full mailboxes.
tldr.outcome: The architecture enabled multi-device mail access for resource-constrained PCs in the mid-1980s but was experimental and not standardized. RFC 993 superseded this proposal.

today: RFC 984 is Historic and was published for discussion only. It represents preliminary experimental thinking on distributed mail for personal computers and was superseded by RFC 993. It provides insight into the challenges of multi-device mail in resource-constrained environments.

sections.title: PCMAIL Architecture Overview
sections.content:
PCMAIL is a distributed mail system for personal computers designed around the constraints of 1980s PCs: they are inexpensive (enabling multiple devices per user), portable (often disconnected), and resource-poor (limited memory and storage).

The system has two halves. The repository is a central storage server holding all incoming mail and maintaining the authoritative global mail state. The clients are PC applications that maintain a local mail state (a local copy of mail) and synchronize it with the repository.

Clients communicate with the repository via the Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP). All DMSP operations are atomic: they either succeed completely or fail completely. Abrupt client disconnections never leave inconsistent or damaged mail states.
sections.eli5: The repository is the main mail office that never closes. Your PC is a local office that syncs with the main office whenever it is connected. Both sides keep a copy, so you can work offline.

sections.title: Repository Structure and Data Model
sections.content:
The repository manages users via user objects, each holding a unique name, password, a list of client objects, and a list of mailbox objects.

Client objects identify each PC a user owns and track its status (active or inactive). Inactive clients are those not connecting for a week; when they reconnect, the repository marks all messages as changed, forcing a complete resynchronization (faster than tracking incremental changes over a week).

Messages are stored in mailboxes and split into two parts: a descriptor (about 100 bytes) containing the UID, size, date, from, to, subject, and system and user-defined flags; and a body containing the RFC-822 message header and text. Mailbox objects describe each mailbox's total messages, unseen messages, and next available UID.

For incoming Internet mail, address objects map RFC-822-style addresses to (user-name, mailbox-name) pairs so the repository can route Internet mail to the correct user and mailbox.
sections.eli5: The repository knows about each user, each of their machines, and each of their mailboxes. It splits every message into a tiny card catalog entry and the full letter so small machines can at least see what mail they have.

sections.title: DMSP: The Communication Protocol
sections.content:
DMSP is a block-stream protocol implemented on top of the Unified Stream Protocol (USP). USP provides a reliable virtual circuit connection and defines basic data types (strings, integers, booleans, etc.). DMSP operations are made of one or more USP blocks, each identified by a numeric block type.

A DMSP session begins with the client opening a connection and authenticating itself and its user via login. The user then performs mail operations before logging out. Operations fall into categories: general operations (abort, debug control, version check, message sending); user operations (login, logout, add/remove users, change password); client operations (list, add, or remove clients, reset client); mailbox operations (list, add, remove, expunge, reset mailboxes); address operations (list, add, or remove address mappings); and message operations (get/set message flags, get descriptors, copy messages, print messages).

All operations require explicit acknowledgement: state modifications return OK or failure; information requests return the requested data.
sections.eli5: The client connects, logs in, does a list of jobs (send mail, flag read, delete, sync), then logs out. Everything is confirmed so nothing gets lost if the connection breaks.

sections.title: Client Modes: Batch and Interactive
sections.content:
PCMAIL supports two client modes tailored to PC connectivity patterns.

Interactive mode is for clients always connected to the network. User changes to local mail state are immediately transmitted and applied to the repository's global state. New incoming mail is immediately sent to the client.

Batch mode is for infrequently-connected clients. Users manipulate the local mail state offline, queuing changes as actions. When the client connects, all actions are transmitted and the local state is synchronized with the repository's global state in one batch.

This two-mode design allows a single DMSP implementation to serve both permanently-connected and nomadic users efficiently.
sections.eli5: Always-on clients get updates immediately. Occasionally-connected clients bundle up all their changes and sync them all at once when they plug in.

sections.title: Synchronization and Message Descriptors
sections.content:
Since client storage is limited, clients may not hold complete message bodies. PCMAIL allows clients to hold a complete list of descriptors (message summaries) while message bodies are fetched on demand.

Synchronization is the critical problem. When a repository mail state changes—new mail arrives or another client modifies a message—the repository tracks which clients need to know about the change via an update list. When a client connects, it requests changed descriptors via get-changed-descriptors. The repository sends descriptors on the client's update list. The client stores them locally and calls reset-changed-descriptors to remove itself from the update list.

In this way, a client can iterate through mailboxes, fetch what changed, incorporate the changes, and mark everything synchronized. Interactive clients can poll for changes at intervals; batch clients synchronize once per session.
sections.eli5: The repository notes which machines have not seen each change. When a machine asks 'What is new?', the repository sends only what that machine has not seen yet. Once the machine updates, it says 'I got it' and the repository stops sending that.

sections.title: Typical Client-Repository Session
sections.content:
A typical session shows how PCMAIL works in practice. A client for user Fred logs in with credentials and client name. The repository checks authentication and responds OK (or FORCE-RESET if the client was inactive for over a week).

Fred's client asks for the mailbox list. The repository returns mailboxes with their message counts, unseen counts, and next UIDs. This summary lets the client see what mail exists without pulling bodies.

The client requests up to N changed descriptors. The repository returns descriptors (message summaries) that have changed since Fred's client last synchronized, along with information about expunged messages. The client incorporates these into its local state and calls reset-changed-descriptors to record that it has seen them.

The client can then set message flags (mark read, delete, forward), copy messages to other mailboxes, or request message bodies via get-message-text. All operations return OK or failure. Finally, the client logs out.
sections.eli5: Fred logs in. He asks 'What mailboxes do I have?' and learns how many unread messages are in each. He asks 'What is new since I was last on?' The repository lists new and changed messages. Fred reads them, marks some as important, deletes spam, and logs out.
